question: Which blood type is known as the universal donor?
explanation: O negative red cells carry none of the main antigens, so almost any patient can receive them in an emergency.

question: Which element is the most abundant in the Earth's crust by mass?
explanation: Oxygen makes up roughly 46 percent of the crust, locked away in silicates and oxides rather than floating around as gas.

question: Which subatomic particle was identified first?
explanation: J. J. Thomson pinned down the electron in 1897, decades before the neutron turned up in 1932.

question: Sound travels faster through water than through air.
explanation: Sound moves at about 1,500 metres per second in water, roughly four times its speed in air, because water is far less squishy.

question: On average, how many thousands of kilometres is the Moon from Earth?
explanation: The Moon orbits at an average 384,400 km, far enough that every planet in the solar system could be lined up in the gap.

question: The Rosetta Stone was the key to deciphering which ancient writing system?
explanation: The same decree carved in Greek and two Egyptian scripts let scholars finally crack hieroglyphs in the 1820s.

question: The Treaty of Ghent, signed in 1814, ended which conflict?
explanation: News travelled so slowly that the Battle of New Orleans was fought two weeks after peace had already been signed.

question: Who is traditionally named as the last emperor of the Western Roman Empire?
explanation: A teenager whose name combined Rome's legendary founder and its first emperor was deposed in 476.

question: The Great Fire of London in 1666 officially recorded fewer than ten deaths.
explanation: Only a handful of deaths were ever recorded, though the fire destroyed some 13,000 houses.

question: Put these events in chronological order, earliest first.
option1: Magna Carta is sealed at Runnymede
correctAnswer: Magna Carta is sealed at Runnymede|The Black Death reaches England|Constantinople falls to the Ottomans|Columbus reaches the Caribbean
explanation: The run goes 1215, 1348, 1453 and 1492, so the Middle Ages ended with two hammer blows just 39 years apart.

question: Which of these South American countries is landlocked?
explanation: Bolivia lost its coastline to Chile in the 19th century and still keeps a navy on Lake Titicaca.

question: Which African country is completely surrounded by South Africa?
explanation: Lesotho is one of only three countries entirely enclosed by a single neighbour, along with San Marino and Vatican City.

question: Which African country shares land borders with the most other countries?
explanation: The DR Congo touches nine neighbours, from Angola in the south-west all the way round to South Sudan.

question: The northernmost point of mainland Africa lies further north than the southernmost point of mainland Europe.
explanation: Cape Angela in Tunisia sits above 37 degrees north, while Spain's Punta de Tarifa is just under 36 degrees.

question: How deep is Challenger Deep, the lowest known point of the ocean, in metres?
explanation: Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench is roughly 10,935 metres down, deep enough to swallow Everest with a mile to spare.

question: Whose record-shattering concert film was titled The Eras Tour?
explanation: The Eras Tour film opened in October 2023 and became the highest-grossing concert movie ever, spanning Taylor Swift's whole back catalogue.

question: Which video game hero was originally known simply as Jumpman?
explanation: He was Jumpman in 1981's Donkey Kong before Nintendo renamed him Mario, reportedly after their US warehouse landlord.

question: In The Simpsons, what was the name of Ned Flanders' late wife?
explanation: Maude Flanders was killed by a T-shirt cannon at a racetrack in 2000, written out after a contract dispute with her voice actor.

question: James Earl Jones went uncredited as the voice of Darth Vader when the first Star Wars was released.
explanation: He felt the role was really David Prowse's body work and asked for no credit, only taking one from The Empire Strikes Back onwards.

question: Which director made Pulp Fiction, Jackie Brown and Kill Bill?
explanation: Quentin Tarantino famously learned his craft behind the counter of a California video rental shop rather than at film school.

question: In ten-pin bowling, what is the nickname for three strikes in a row?
explanation: The name is said to come from 19th-century tournaments that handed out live turkeys as prizes for three strikes.

question: The FIVB is the international governing body for which Olympic sport?
explanation: FIVB stands for Federation Internationale de Volleyball, which also runs the beach version of the game.

question: Which nation has won the most Olympic gold medals in field hockey?
explanation: India has eight hockey golds, including six in a row from 1928 to 1956.

question: The Olympic marathon has always been run over the modern distance of 26.2 miles.
explanation: Early Olympic marathons ranged from about 24 to 26 miles, and 26 miles 385 yards was only fixed as standard from 1924.

question: How many stitches are there on a standard Major League Baseball?
explanation: Every big-league ball is hand-stitched with exactly 108 double stitches of waxed red thread.

question: In computing, what does USB stand for?
explanation: Universal Serial Bus arrived in 1996 to replace the tangle of ports on the back of every PC.

question: What was the first item ever sold on eBay, back in 1995?
explanation: It went for 14.83 dollars, and the buyer confirmed he collected broken laser pointers on purpose.

question: The world's first webcam was set up at Cambridge University to watch what?
explanation: The Trojan Room coffee pot was filmed so researchers could avoid climbing stairs to find an empty jug.

question: The first message sent over ARPANET failed partway through, so only two letters arrived.
explanation: They tried to send LOGIN in 1969 but the system crashed after LO, making it the internet's first accidental greeting.

question: Put these gadgets in order of their original release, earliest first.
correctAnswer: Sony Walkman|Nintendo Game Boy|Apple iPod|Amazon Kindle
explanation: Walkman 1979, Game Boy 1989, iPod 2001 and Kindle 2007 - roughly a decade apart each time, until the 2000s sped up.

question: Which artist painted the melting pocket watches of The Persistence of Memory?
explanation: Dali said the drooping watches were inspired by camembert cheese softening in the sun.

question: What is the technique of painting onto freshly laid wet plaster called?
explanation: In true fresco the pigment bonds with the drying plaster, so the painting becomes part of the wall itself.

question: The pigment name ultramarine literally means what?
explanation: It was ground from lapis lazuli shipped to Europe from Afghanistan, so it arrived from beyond the sea.

question: Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling lying flat on his back.
explanation: He worked standing on custom scaffolding, craning backwards, which wrecked his neck but never had him lying down.

question: Which Mexican painter is famous for fierce self-portraits featuring flowers, monkeys and a joined brow?
explanation: Frida Kahlo painted around 55 self-portraits, once saying she painted herself because she was so often alone.

question: Which author created the Discworld series, set on a flat world carried by elephants on a giant turtle?
explanation: Terry Pratchett wrote 41 Discworld novels, and his hat and sword were later famously part of his estate.

question: Which Nigerian writer is best known for the 1958 novel Things Fall Apart?
explanation: Achebe took his title from a Yeats poem, and the book has since sold over 20 million copies in some 60 languages.

question: Which of the Bronte sisters published under the pen name Currer Bell?
explanation: Charlotte was Currer, Emily was Ellis and Anne was Acton, all keeping the deliberately ambiguous Bell surname.

question: Mary Shelley was still a teenager when she began writing Frankenstein.
explanation: She was 18 during the famous ghost-story challenge at Lake Geneva in 1816 and only 20 when the novel appeared.

question: Which author wrote the 1932 dystopian novel Brave New World?
explanation: Huxley imagined a society drugged on soma and sorted into castes, and he died on the same day as C.S. Lewis and JFK.

question: How many strings does a standard ukulele have?
explanation: A standard ukulele has four strings, usually tuned G-C-E-A, which is why chords are so easy for beginners.

question: Which instrument earned the jazz-era nickname the licorice stick?
explanation: Its slim black body reminded players of a licorice stick, and the name stuck all through the swing era.

question: Who played the famous saxophone riff on Gerry Rafferty's Baker Street?
explanation: Session player Raphael Ravenscroft recorded the riff for a modest session fee and later said his cheque bounced.

question: The theremin is played without the performer ever touching the instrument.
explanation: Players move their hands in the electromagnetic fields around two antennas to control pitch and volume, never touching it.

question: Put these music formats in order of when they were first introduced, earliest first.
explanation: The LP arrived in 1948, the cassette in 1963, the CD in 1982 and the iPod in 2001 - roughly one leap per generation.

question: Which spice is the most expensive in the world by weight?
explanation: Saffron is hand-picked from crocus flowers, and it takes roughly 150,000 blooms to make a single kilogram.

question: The green paste served as wasabi in most restaurants is usually made mainly from what?
explanation: Real wasabi rhizome is notoriously hard to grow, so dyed horseradish stands in for it almost everywhere.

question: Which French mother sauce is built from a white roux and milk?
explanation: Bechamel is the milk-based mother sauce, while veloute uses stock and espagnole uses brown stock.

question: Ketchup began life as a fermented fish sauce rather than a tomato product.
explanation: The word comes from a Southeast Asian fermented fish condiment, and tomatoes were not added until the 1800s.

question: What is the name of the savoury fifth basic taste, identified by a Japanese chemist in 1908?
explanation: Kikunae Ikeda isolated glutamate from kombu dashi and coined umami, meaning delicious taste.
